title: Randomized trial at Korea University and Ewha Womans University hospitals: ENAD-DET-01 raises adenoma detection from 36.1% to 52.3%
summary: In a two-hospital Seoul trial of 998 patients, colonoscopy with Ainex's ENAD-DET-01 found adenomas in 52.3% of patients against 36.1% with standard colonoscopy.
account: Gastroenterologists at Korea University College of Medicine and Ewha Womans University College of Medicine ran a randomized trial at two tertiary hospitals in Seoul, South Korea, from May 2023 to April 2025. They randomly assigned 998 adults who had screening, surveillance or diagnostic colonoscopy to colonoscopy with or without ENAD-DET-01, a deep-learning detection system from Ainex Corporation of Seoul. The system draws a circle on the endoscopy monitor when it recognizes a polyp. Adenomas were found in 52.3% of patients in the system group and in 36.1% of the control group. Polyps were found in 72.2% against 54.5%, and the system group had 1.2 adenomas per colonoscopy against 0.8. The system did not raise the detection of sessile serrated lesions or cancers. Both hospitals used the same Olympus endoscopy platform. The Korea Medical Device Development Fund paid for the study, and the authors report no conflicts of interest.
purpose: ENAD-DET-01 was built to detect colorectal polyps on the live colonoscopy video. The higher adenoma detection was that purpose.
deployer: Korea University Medical Center and Ewha Womans University Medical Center

The paper states that the system receives digital input directly from the endoscopy processor and that both centers used the same colonoscopy system from Olympus. H. J. Jeon and colleagues, Gut and Liver, November 27, 2025, methods section. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12800677/
brief: A randomized trial has tested ENAD-DET-01, a polyp-detection system from the South Korean company Ainex. At two Seoul hospitals between May 2023 and April 2025, 998 patients were assigned at random to colonoscopy with or without the system, which draws a circle on the monitor when it detects a polyp. Adenomas were found in 52.3% of patients with the system and 36.1% without.[1] For sessile serrated lesions and cancers, the difference between the groups was not statistically significant. A control rate of 36.1% left room for improvement, and units that already detect more may see a smaller gain. Elsewhere, researchers found no gain in a randomized trial of computer-aided polyp detection at a Japanese community hospital. Both hospitals used one Olympus platform, so the trial does not test the system on other equipment.[2] The Korea Medical Device Development Fund paid for the study, and the authors report no conflicts of interest.
